title: Croatia Buys 18 Hanwha Chunmoo Launchers as Europe Shifts to Korean Artillery; Ukraine Seeks EU Funds for First Patriot Buy
subhead: Zagreb's €544 million K239 Chunmoo order — its second major artillery purchase after HIMARS — underscores a European pivot to South Korean systems as US delivery delays bite. Separately, Kyiv is asking Brussels to waive its €90 billion loan rules so it can buy US-made PAC-3 interceptors for the first time.

sections.heading: Croatia Orders 18 Hanwha K239 Chunmoo Launchers in €544M Deal
sections.body: The Croatian government has approved the acquisition of 18 K239 Chunmoo multiple-rocket launchers from South Korea's Hanwha Aerospace, worth around €544.1 million ($631.9 million), with deliveries scheduled for 2026 to 2029, Defense News reports. Defense Minister Ivan Anušić cited 'relatively short delivery times of 24 to 36 months, better availability, lower prices, openness to industrial cooperation' as reasons European countries are choosing the system. Hanwha's Polish partner WB Group will supply the command-and-control system. The launchers replace Croatia's aging Yugoslav-era M-92 Vulkan and Soviet-designed GRAD BM-21 systems, and follow Zagreb's December 2024 purchase of eight US HIMARS launchers worth about $351 million.
sections.whyItMatters: Croatia joins Poland, Estonia and Norway in buying the Chunmoo as an alternative to Lockheed Martin's HIMARS. The pattern is driven by US delivery delays flagged after the Iran war — including HIMARS ammunition — and signals South Korea's Hanwha is consolidating a European foothold in rocket artillery at Lockheed's expense.

sections.heading: Ukraine Asks EU to Fund First Patriot Missiles Buy
sections.body: Ukraine has formally asked the European Union to let it spend part of its €90 billion support loan on US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its Patriot batteries — the first time Kyiv has sought to tap the fund for American systems, Defense News reports. The loan's rules cap non-EU/Ukrainian content at 35% of a purchase's value, so the request needs a formal exemption. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Sept. 2 the review 'is moving in the right direction,' with EU representatives due to decide on the waiver Monday. Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said Ukraine faces a $27 billion defense budget deficit and pressed partners to fund Ukrainian drone production and resume talks on using frozen Russian assets.
sections.whyItMatters: The request tests whether Europe's 'buy European' defense-loan rules can bend under wartime pressure. Kyiv already won a similar carve-out in April for Chinese-made drone components, and a PAC-3 exemption would set a precedent for routing EU money to US defense firms — a politically sensitive step as Washington separately seeks repayment from Europe for past Ukraine aid.

sections.heading: US Air Force Accelerates Cheaper Reaper Successor After Iran Losses
sections.body: The US Air Force is pulling forward its timeline for a cheaper, more expendable successor to the MQ-9A Reaper after combat losses, officials said Sept. 3, Defense News reports. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink directed the acceleration, with the fiscal 2031 target of 20 mission-ready aircraft possibly moved up by about two years. The Washington Post reported Aug. 13 that at least 45 Reapers had been lost — roughly 25% of the fleet — since operations against Iran began in February. The follow-on, the Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), opened as a Defense Innovation Unit competition in July, seeking a drone with at least 2,800 pounds of payload and an 8,000-nautical-mile ferry range. Chief modernization officer Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi priced MMA air vehicles near $10 million, about half the roughly $20 million cost of a Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
sections.whyItMatters: The Reaper's attrition in the Iran war is reshaping US drone procurement toward expendability over sophistication. With General Atomics having shut MQ-9A production in 2025, the Air Force cannot easily backfill — pushing it to embrace a mass-producible, loss-tolerant design that marks a philosophical break from the high-cost Reaper model.

sections.heading: US and Russia Opposition Threatens Autonomous Weapons Talks in Geneva
sections.body: Diplomats say US and Russian opposition has raised doubts that the 128 states party to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) will agree in Geneva on a text that could pave the way to international rules on lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS), Defense News/Reuters report. A majority of countries support a draft, but Washington and Moscow have proposed late changes and deletions. The US position has hardened over the past six months, favoring guidelines over a legally binding treaty, a position supported by Russia, India and Turkey. Backers of a binding treaty — including Brazil, Ireland and several African states — argue safeguards are needed to ensure meaningful human control. In August, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and Red Cross President Mirjana Spoljaric warned the world was nearing a moral red line where autonomous weapons could kill without human involvement.
sections.whyItMatters: The talks test whether the international community can constrain AI-enabled weapons at a moment when semi-autonomous systems are already being used in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East. With the US and Russia aligned against binding rules, the likely outcome is a weak, non-binding document — leaving the regulatory vacuum intact as autonomous capability spreads.

sections.heading: Northrop Grumman Wins $508.5M Missile Defense Target Contract; $862M Artillery Kits
sections.body: Northrop Grumman was awarded a $508.5 million Missile Defense Agency contract to provide flight test support for intermediate-range ballistic missile and ICBM targets, ClearanceJobs reported Sept. 6. Separately, the Department of War's Sept. 3 contract round included an $862 million Northrop Grumman award for M1156 precision guidance kits for Army artillery, a $194 million General Dynamics contract for technical support on the nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile program's fire control subsystem, and a $40.7 million Dynetics award for medium-range air defense radar systems, per DefenseHub's OSINT summary.
sections.whyItMatters: The MDA target contract keeps the pipeline of realistic ballistic-missile test targets flowing as the US expands missile defense under the Golden Dome initiative. The artillery guidance-kit award reflects the Pentagon's push to convert conventional shells into precision munitions — a priority sharpened by the Iran war's heavy ammunition consumption.

sections.heading: India's Fighter Engine Contest: Rolls-Royce and Safran Vie for AMCA Mk-2
sections.body: India's plan to co-develop a high-thrust engine for its fifth-generation fighter has set up a contest between British and French aerospace firms, Defense News reports. Rolls-Royce and Reliance Industries announced 'strategic intent' this month to jointly develop and manufacture an indigenous engine, including exploring a dedicated aerospace gas-turbine complex in India. France's Safran has separately proposed co-developing a high-thrust engine with India's state-run Gas Turbine Research Establishment for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), with its offer under evaluation by the Cabinet Committee on Security. Both offer full technology transfer and Indian ownership of intellectual property. The initial AMCA variants will use the American GE F414 engine, but the Mk-2 needs a foreign partner for a 120 kN-class turbofan.
sections.whyItMatters: India is seeking to end its decades-long dependence on foreign fighter engines — a capability held by only a handful of countries. The Rolls-Royce-Reliance tie-up and Safran's offer both promise full tech transfer, making this a rare case where New Delhi can extract sovereign engine capability from Western industry as it builds toward strategic autonomy.

sections.heading: India Opens Conventional Missile Technology to Private Sector
sections.body: India has approved transferring technology for all conventional missile systems from state-run organizations to private companies, Defense News reports, citing the defense ministry, which called the move an 'important milestone.' The decision broadens the industrial base for missile manufacturing as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed the difficulty of replenishing missile and ammunition stocks. Analysts said the move reflects lessons from those conflicts and India's brief four-day conflict with Pakistan last year. The government did not identify which systems are covered, but reports suggest a broad range from air-defense to air-to-air and surface-to-surface missiles.
sections.whyItMatters: New Delhi is deliberately widening its missile production base beyond state-owned firms, betting that private industry can scale output faster. The move mirrors a global lesson from the Iran and Ukraine wars: stockpile replenishment, not just development, is the binding constraint in modern conflict.

bottomLine: Today's defense industry news is dominated by the fallout of the Iran war on procurement. Croatia's €544 million Chunmoo order shows European buyers diversifying away from US systems amid delivery delays, while Ukraine's request to tap EU funds for US-made PAC-3 interceptors tests whether Europe's buy-local rules can bend under wartime pressure. The US Air Force's accelerated push for a cheaper, expendable Reaper successor reflects the war's attrition on high-cost drones, and the Geneva autonomous-weapons talks look set to produce a weak outcome as the US and Russia align against binding rules. India, meanwhile, is moving to build sovereign missile and engine capability by opening technology to private industry and courting Western partners.
sources: Defense News, Reuters, ClearanceJobs, DefenseHub OSINT, Washington Post, Breaking Defense, Defense Daily
